pr_title: ports/esp32/machine_timer.c: Solves #4078, ESP32 timer reinitilization error
pr_body:
Solves the problem where multiple calls to `machine.Timer.init()` causes an `OSError 261` on ESP32 boards.

The fix is explained here: https://github.com/espressif/arduino-esp32/issues/1869#issuecomment-423016007

Solves issue #4078.
pr_comments: Thanks for the patch, but I'm not sure it's the right way to solve that issue of error 261.  Active timers are put on a linked list (on the MicroPython side) and if you create a timer twice then it'll be placed twice on this list.  I think it would be better to check for an existing timer on the list when creating one, and reuse it if found.

Oh yes, didn't actually think of that! But now when checking the code, I don't believe that's the case. 

The init function calls machine_timer_disable which removes the existing timer from the list, before changing parameters and reenabling it.

https://github.com/micropython/micropython/blob/master/ports/esp32/machine_timer.c#L179

> The init function calls machine_timer_disable which removes the existing timer from the list, before changing parameters and reenabling it.

But that doesn't stop there being multiple instances of Timer all pointing to the same underlying hardware resource, because these multiple Timer instances are distinct pointers to the MicroPython heap.

Okay, I see. I can implement a reference counting solution. Just as a sanity check before I start, do you think the following would be a suitable solution:

 - Timer's are added to the list already in the Timer constructor, not by the .init() method, if added twice reference counter is increased and the existing timer returned.
 - Timer's are stopped started by .init() / .deinit() method, but does not alter the list
 - Timer's are removed from the list in `__del__` (or -1 ref count)

Btw. I still believe the flags in the patch are necessary though, to solve the problem that occurs in programs such as this, which also raises OSError 261:
```python
timer0 = Timer(0)
timer0.init(period=1000, mode=Timer.PERIODIC, callback=my_callback)
timer0.deinit()
timer0.init(period=1000, mode=Timer.PERIODIC, callback=my_callback)
```

> I can implement a reference counting solution.

I don't think it needs that.  There are only 4 timers in total so just keeping them in the link list forever after creation is fine (until soft reset, via `machine_timer_deinit_all()`).  Adding them to the list in the constructor sounds good.


>  I still believe the flags in the patch are necessary though, to solve the problem that occurs in programs such as this, which also raises OSError 261

That particular code runs fine for me, no error.

Okay, check the latest commit. 

You are right, the flags are not necessary. The example raising OSError 261 above only appeared when re-executing the code after a soft-reboot, however, it works now without the flags.

issue_context.title: Getting  OSError 261 from machine.Timer on esp32
issue_context.body:
Probably too obscure to worry about but I diagnosed the following problem in the Timer Module on the esp32.

If you mistakenly initialize two Timer objects with the same ID, all timers created after the error fail and report "OSError 261".  Unhelpfully, the Timer objects get created without errors and only fail when you run `mytimer.init(...)`

The code below all works except for the lines followed by error messages.

def mycallback(tmr):
   print(tmr)

from machine import Timer
t1 = Timer(200)
t2 = Timer(201)
t1.init(period=2000, mode=Timer.ONE_SHOT, callback=mycallback)
t2.init(period=2000, mode=Timer.ONE_SHOT, callback=mycallback)
t2 = Timer(201)
t2.init(period=2000, mode=Timer.ONE_SHOT, callback=mycallback)
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "<stdin>", line 1, in <module>
OSError: 261

t3 = Timer(205)
t4 = Timer(206)
t1.init(period=2000, mode=Timer.ONE_SHOT, callback=mycallback)
t3.init(period=2000, mode=Timer.ONE_SHOT, callback=mycallback)
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "<stdin>", line 1, in <module>
OSError: 261
t2.init(period=2000, mode=Timer.ONE_SHOT, callback=mycallback)
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "<stdin>", line 1, in <module>
OSError: 261
comments:
Same situation happened to me.
For ESP32 is only one timer (-1).
If you are use more then one ESP got stuck.

I also got OSError: 261 on esp32 and using Machine.Timer.

In my case, It happened when I was troubleshooting and so hitting Ctrl-D often.
I noticed that when I did machine.reset() it no longer happened.
I was using timer 0

I was ending my main.py with a timer so that I could test things on the command line.  

```
timer = Timer(0)
timer.init(period=60000, mode=Timer.PERIODIC, callback=lambda t:cb_refine())
```

after pressing Ctrl-D the OSerror: 261 happens when it reaches this line again for the second time.

> Traceback (most recent call last):
>   File "main.py", line 64, in <module>
> OSError: 261
> MicroPython v1.10 on 2019-01-25; ESP32 module with ESP32
I just changed it from Timer(0) to  Timer(-1), Timer(1), Timer(2) and Timer(3) and all exhibit the same problem when using soft reset or Ctrl-D.
Also I used timer.deinit() before Ctrl-D and the issue goes away.

In my test, it is nothing related to timer.deinit().
I can reproduce by following procedure:
1. Hardware Reset
2. Download Run (for example: timer_test.py)
3. reFlush tree Error
4. reconnect UART
5. 			               <---Auto run step2 timer_test.py (I don't know why)
6. Stop
7. Download Run
8. Stop
9. Download Run		<--OSError 261

I suspect that this issue is cause by "STOP" command will not reset system, therefore when I donwnload and run again, it will cause two identical timer ID running on the background, then generate OSError:261.

Is it reasonable ?

PS. IDE is uPyCraft v1.1

Adding the following timer allocation flags to the call to `timer_isr_register` in ports/esp32/machine_timer.c solves the issue (also explained here: https://github.com/espressif/arduino-esp32/issues/1869 )

```#define TIMER_FLAGS    (ESP_INTR_FLAG_LOWMED | ESP_INTR_FLAG_SHARED)```

I have tested it works with all timers and will make a pull request.

review_comments: Does this need a `MP_STATE_PORT(machine_timer_obj_head) = NULL` at the end?
Good catch, my C is rusty after many years in the FP world. I have commited a small fix.
